title: Artificial intelligence (AI)-triggered rapid response notifications were associated with lower mortality among inpatients
key_facts: Nahass and colleagues studied an AI-powered electronic alert system that automatically notifies the rapid response team (RRT) when the Epic Deterioration Index (EDI) risk score reaches at least 60.
The study covered adult admissions at 11 hospital sites: 10,803 patients before the system went live (scores calculated but not used) and 12,329 afterward.
Unadjusted in-hospital mortality fell from 23.1% to 18.6% (2,500 deaths versus 2,297), an absolute difference of 4.5 percentage points; the adjusted odds ratio for death was 0.82 (95% CI 0.74-0.91).
Rapid response activations rose from 25.3% to 37.5%; escalation to higher-level care did not rise significantly.
Only 46.6% of post-implementation encounters produced a notification, because some were filtered out (for example existing intensive or comfort care, or recent alerts).
For patients just below the threshold (EDI 55-59) the adjusted odds ratio was 0.99 (95% CI 0.70-1.39); just above it was 0.86 (95% CI 0.63-1.17).
Limits: unequal seasonal distribution of the before and after periods, incomplete implementation at two hospitals, and uncertain generalizability beyond the sites studied.
quote_evidence: Automated rapid response team notifications were associated with lower inpatient deaths and more rapid response activations.
The study found that unadjusted mortality decreased from 23.1% before implementation to 18.6% afterward, with an adjusted odds ratio of 0.82.
This study was limited by unequal seasonal distributions of the pre- and post-intervention phases, incomplete implementation at two hospitals, and uncertain generalizability beyond the sites studied.
why_it_matters_hint: Linking an AI deterioration score to automatic alerts for the response team was associated with fewer deaths among high-risk inpatients, in a before-and-after comparison.
event_date: Not stated; the article does not name the journal or the study's publication date. 2 Minute Medicine published 3 Oct 2026.
notes: One outlet summarising a study; the journal and any outside review are not named. Before-and-after design, not a randomised trial; the near-threshold comparison was not conclusive. The Epic Deterioration Index is a tool from Epic (see C10-01).
